newsitem.title: ITALY: SOCCER-NIZZOLA TO HEAD ITALIAN SOCCER FEDERATION.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-NIZZOLA TO HEAD ITALIAN SOCCER FEDERATION.

text.p: The feuding chairmen of Italy's soccer leagues struck a deal on Monday to end a vacuum at the top of the country's federation, leaderless since a bitter election battle failed to produce a winner.

Federation sources said the accord would lead to the election of Lega Calcio (football league) chairman Luciano Nizzola as president of the Italian Soccer Federation (FIGC) with Serie C chairman Giancarlo Abete as vice-president.
The two men were rivals for the top post last month after incumbent Antonio Matarrese stepped down but two rounds of voting ended in embarrassing deadlock.
The federation has since been run by an emergency commissioner, Raffaele Pagnozzi, who was appointed by the Italian Olympic Committee.

The sources said Monday's deal would be put in writing by Pagnozzi, who helped strike the compromise in an hour of closed door talks with Nizzola, Abete and the chairman of the Italian amateur league, Elio Giulivi.
It will lead to a fresh election between December 9 and 14 that should ensure Nizzola wins the required backing of one third of the clubs in each league.

"There are neither winners nor losers," Nizzola said after the meeting, which took place at the Coverciano training ground near Florence where Italy are preparing for World Cup qualifiers against Moldova and Georgia this month.
"We have made a great deal of progress and it's clear to the commissioner that the basis exists for resolving this crisis rapidly," Nizzola said.
Abete said he was satisfied with the outcome.

Matarrese came under intense pressure after Italy crashed out of the European championship in June. He stepped down last month after eight years as federation president in the face of a challenge from Nizzola.
Nizzola had the backing of Serie A and Serie B clubs and looked a certain winner until Abete entered the fray with the unanimous backing of his minor league clubs.
The resultant deadlock and the subsequent appointment of a special commissioner for only the fourth time in almost 100 years of Italian soccer were branded a fiasco by Italian sports newspapers.
